props.title: Fantômas

sections.content: **Fantômas (1913)** (1913) revolutionized early cinema's approach to serialized storytelling and criminal anti-heroes. Director Louis Feuillade crafted five feature-length episodes following the exploits of the masked criminal mastermind Fantômas, played with magnetic menace by René Navarre. The series directly influenced **The Cabinet of Dr. Caligari** (1920) and **Dr. Mabuse the Gambler** (1922) with its blend of psychological horror and criminal intrigue. Feuillade's innovative use of Paris locations and real architecture created a documentary-like authenticity that contrasted brilliantly with the supernatural elements of the story.

sections.content: The influence of **Fantômas** (1913) extends far beyond early cinema. The character inspired the French New Wave, with directors like François Truffaut citing it as a major influence. The series' blend of realism and fantastical elements echoes through **Batman** (1989), **V for Vendetta** (2005), and modern superhero cinema. The masked criminal genius archetype Feuillade established became a template for countless thriller antagonists.

Feuillade's innovative cinematography and staging created a visual language that still resonates. His use of depth staging, where action unfolds across multiple planes within the frame, influenced directors from Fritz Lang to Christopher Nolan. The rooftop chase sequences in **Fantômas** (1913) prefigure similar scenes in everything from **Vertigo** (1958) to **The Matrix** (1999). SUBHEAD: Legacy in Crime Cinema

The series' impact on crime films cannot be overstated. The cat-and-mouse game between Fantômas and Inspector Juve established tropes still used in detective fiction. **The Third Man** (1949) draws clear inspiration from Feuillade's use of urban architecture as a character, while **M** (1931) echoes the series' exploration of criminal psychology and urban paranoia. Modern films like **Drive** (2011) continue to reference the visual style and moral ambiguity pioneered by **Fantômas**.
